strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in style-personalized text-to-image generation: transferring the style of a single reference image without per-style training. The focus on a scale-wise autoregressive backbone is useful because most prior style-personalization work is diffusion-based and often slow or requires fine-tuning.

The proposed method is technically simple and plausible: identify an influential early generation step, use SVD-based principal feature blending to inject style information, and use structural attention correction to stabilize content structure. The inference-only nature and frozen Infinity-2B backbone make the method attractive for deployment.

The paper provides a coherent empirical story. The step-wise prompt injection analysis, SVD manipulation analysis, PFB/SAC ablations, alpha ablation, and qualitative examples generally support the authors' design choices.

The reported efficiency is a meaningful practical advantage. The method generates a 1024x1024 image in 3.58 seconds on an A6000, substantially faster than the compared diffusion and tuning-based baselines, while achieving competitive harmonic CLIP score.

The evaluation includes several relevant baselines, including IP-Adapter, StyleAligned, StyleDrop, DreamStyler, DB-LoRA, B-LoRA, CSGO, and StyleAR, plus a user study with 30 participants. The supplementary results also show qualitative transfer to Infinity-8B and Switti.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than decisive. The method builds directly on Infinity and resembles a natural extension of prior scale-wise AR style-control ideas; the main algorithmic contribution is a targeted SVD feature replacement plus attention copying. This is elegant, but the paper does not fully establish that the underlying insight is deep or broadly general beyond the chosen architecture family.

The quantitative gains are not very strong. The proposed method has harmonic score 0.437, slightly below StyleAligned at 0.438 and only marginally above StyleAR at 0.434 and IP-Adapter at 0.433. Its main advantage is speed and prompt fidelity, not clearly superior overall generation quality.

The evidence for the central style/content decomposition claim is limited. The analysis uses color changes as a proxy for style and CLIP similarities to object/color words; this is a narrow notion of style compared with texture, brushwork, geometry, composition, and artistic medium. It is therefore not fully convincing that the dominant singular component generally captures style rather than a mixture of low-frequency appearance factors.

The comparison protocol may favor the proposed method in runtime reporting. For tuning-based baselines, the table combines per-style tuning time with single-image inference time, which is useful for one-off use but not for amortized generation of many images from the same style. A separate amortized runtime analysis would be needed for a fairer practical comparison.

Evaluation is still narrow for a generative CVPR paper. The benchmark follows FineStyle with 190 prompts and 10 styles, and the metrics are mainly CLIP text/image similarity plus a small user study. There is no broad human evaluation of overall quality, failure rate, content leakage, aesthetic quality, or style consistency across many images per style.

The method depends on style prompts despite being framed as single-reference style personalization. The supplementary material notes that high-level style categories such as oil painting or 3D rendering are used, which weakens the claim that style is extracted purely from the reference image and raises questions about sensitivity to prompt wording.

Reproducibility is partial. The manuscript gives the main equations, step choices, alpha value, backbone, and runtime, but lacks enough low-level implementation detail to reproduce exact results, such as sampling settings, random seed variance, exact prompt list/filtering, style-reference preprocessing, and whether all baselines were run with matched resolutions and decoding settings.

The method has acknowledged limitations for heterogeneous or mixed-style references, and the paper does not provide systematic failure analysis. This matters because real user-provided style references often contain multiple objects, media, layouts, or conflicting visual motifs.

strengths: The paper targets a useful problem: single-reference style personalization without per-style training, and the inference-time framing on a scale-wise autoregressive T2I model is practically appealing.

The proposed modules are simple and lightweight. Principal Feature Blending via SVD and Structural Attention Correction are easy to understand conceptually, and the method reports substantially lower latency than diffusion fine-tuning baselines.

The manuscript includes ablations for feature replacement vs. SVD blending, adding SAC, varying the SVD decay rate, and applying the idea to other scale-wise AR models, which helps support that the components are not entirely incidental.
Qualitative examples suggest the method can often transfer broad color/texture/style cues while preserving prompt content better than some adapter-style baselines.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is weakly supported. The analysis equates style largely with color changes in synthetic prompt pairs, then generalizes this to arbitrary artistic style references. Showing that the top singular component affects color does not convincingly establish that it captures general style rather than global color/appearance statistics.

The method’s exact mechanics are under-specified. The SVD reshape of the feature tensor is not clearly defined, and the SAC algorithm appears to replace queries and keys after the transformer update rather than during self-attention, making the operational implementation ambiguous. This hurts reproducibility and technical confidence.

The quantitative evidence is not strong enough for the claims. In Table 1, the proposed method is not best on harmonic score, style fidelity, or prompt fidelity; its harmonic score is essentially tied with StyleAligned. The paper’s main empirical advantage is speed, but the quality improvements are marginal or metric-dependent.

The runtime comparison is potentially misleading. For fine-tuning methods, the table folds training time into per-image inference time, which exaggerates the advantage if a style is reused to generate multiple images. A fair amortized analysis or separate reporting of adaptation and sampling time is needed.

The evaluation protocol is narrow. It uses only 10 styles and 190 prompts, relies heavily on CLIP-based text/image similarities that are known to be imperfect for style transfer, and lacks stronger perceptual/style metrics, diversity analysis, leakage quantification, or statistical uncertainty.

The user study is insufficiently detailed and only compares against a subset of baselines selected by metric performance. The paper does not report the number of trials, randomization/blinding details, significance tests, or inter-rater consistency, so the human-preference evidence is hard to judge.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. The paper combines familiar ingredients: inference-time feature manipulation, SVD/principal-component filtering, and attention-map correction. The AR-model setting is interesting, but the conceptual novelty is limited unless the claimed feature disentanglement is demonstrated more rigorously.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially statements about precise style extraction, stable structural consistency, and real-time deployment. The method appears useful as a heuristic, but the manuscript presents it as a more principled decomposition than the experiments justify.

Presentation quality is uneven, with grammar issues, cramped figures, and some unclear notation. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they amplify the reproducibility and technical-clarity concerns.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful training-free style-personalization method for scale-wise autoregressive text-to-image generation, targeting an important practical niche: fast single-reference stylization without per-style fine-tuning.

The main technical idea is reasonably well motivated by internal analysis of the AR generation process. The step-wise prompt intervention and SVD-guided feature replacement provide evidence that early features, especially around the third feature/state, carry style-relevant information.

The method is lightweight and conceptually simple: Principal Feature Blending injects dominant style components, while Structural Attention Correction uses the unmodified content stream to reduce structural drift. The ablation study supports the complementary roles of these two modules.

The empirical results show a strong practical advantage in inference speed. The method is far faster than the reported diffusion and fine-tuning baselines while maintaining competitive CLIP harmonic score and strong prompt fidelity.

The evaluation includes several relevant baselines, qualitative comparisons, ablations, a user study, sensitivity analysis for the SVD decay parameter, and qualitative evidence that the approach can transfer to other scale-wise AR models.
weaknesses: The central claim that dominant singular components encode style is supported mainly through color/object prompt manipulations. Color is only a narrow proxy for artistic style, so the evidence does not fully establish that the same decomposition robustly captures texture, stroke, medium, composition, or more complex style attributes.

The quantitative evaluation relies heavily on CLIP-based text/image similarities, which the paper itself notes can be misleading for style fidelity and content leakage. The user study helps, but stronger perceptual or style-specific metrics and more detailed statistical analysis would make the evidence more convincing.

The method appears to use both a reference style image and a style text prompt of the form “<content> in <style>”. This weakens the framing as purely single-reference style personalization unless the dependence on the style prompt is carefully isolated. An ablation without style text, or with mismatched/noisy style descriptions, is missing.

The runtime comparison is favorable but somewhat difficult to interpret. For tuning-based methods, training time is included in the per-image time, which is relevant for one-off personalization but can overstate the advantage when many images are generated per style. Reporting amortized inference-only and setup costs separately would be fairer.

Important implementation details are underspecified for reproducibility, including how the feature tensor is reshaped for SVD, which layers/heads receive SAC, the exact insertion points inside Infinity, random seeds, and whether all baselines use comparable resolutions and prompt formats.

The method is evaluated primarily on a filtered FineStyle-style benchmark with 10 styles and 190 prompts. This is useful but not broad enough to fully support claims of robust style personalization across heterogeneous styles, complex references, or references containing multiple visual motifs.

The reported best harmonic score is essentially tied with StyleAligned rather than clearly better, so the acceptance case rests more on speed, training-free deployment, and qualitative balance than on a decisive quantitative quality improvement.
